flags.line: Ibogaine should be given by trained staff under heart monitoring, considering risk factors like female gender and heart disease.
flags.why: The reviews' recommendation is given as the site's own instruction, with no source named. The editor held run 44648136440 for the same thing; this version (run 44841499696) repeats it.
flags.say: Give a review's recommendation as the review's ('a 2015 review says ibogaine should be given only by trained medical staff, with constant heart monitoring'), never as the site's own instruction.

flags.line: Ibogaine should be given by trained staff under heart monitoring, considering risk factors like female gender and heart disease.
flags.why: Asked about heart attacks, it never says the reviews speak of a dangerous irregular heartbeat (long QT, torsades), nor that no quote shows any step lowers the risk: the monitoring is there to catch and treat it.
flags.say: Name the risk as the sources do (a dangerous irregular heartbeat, not a heart attack), and say plainly that no source shows a step that lowers it; close heart monitoring is how doctors catch it.

flags.line: No. FRANK says every person has a unique experience. Australia's Alcohol and Drug Foundation says effects vary by mood, environment, and health.
flags.why: The question asks whether people who use LSD have traits in common; the answer is about how LSD's effects differ between people. Neither page speaks of who uses LSD, so the 'No.' rests on nothing.
flags.say: Answer the question asked, about the people who use LSD; where no source speaks of them, say so plainly, and never answer 'No' from pages about how the drug's effects vary.

flags.line: Yes. Gabapentinoids can help with nerve issues.
flags.why: The review speaks only of nerve pain ('traditional neuropathic pain indications'); 'nerve issues' stretches it to nerve damage and nerve health, which the question also covers and no quote speaks of.
flags.say: Say what the review says these medicines help, nerve pain, and say plainly that the sources do not speak of other nerve problems.

flags.line: Yes. Gabapentinoids can help with nerve issues.
flags.why: 'Gabapentinoids' (and 'neuropathic pain' in how1) are clinical words where plain ones exist: gabapentin and pregabalin; nerve pain.
flags.say: Name the medicines (gabapentin and pregabalin) and write nerve pain, not gabapentinoids or neuropathic pain.

flags.line: This rests on 1 review and 1 study in people.
flags.why: The second source is a systematic review, and all the answer takes from it (F3 under the short; F3 and F5 under how2) is from animal experiments; 'a study in people' passes animal results off as results in people.
flags.say: Do not rest an answer about people on animal experiments; where one is used, say plainly that it was done in animals.

flags.line: It is involved in opioid-related adverse drug reactions.
flags.why: 'Adverse drug reactions' is a clinical phrase (so are 'adverse reactions' in how2 and 'toxicological case data' in how3), and the line never says what the risk is; F6 names hospital stays and deaths.
flags.say: Say the risk in plain words, as the review does: tramadol is among the opioids often involved in harmful reactions, including ones that put people in hospital or ended in death.

flags.line: Naltrexone may not work for everyone, so it is important to consult a doctor or alcohol and other drug (AOD) counsellor.
flags.why: Advice given in the site's own voice: the words are the Alcohol and Drug Foundation's, but the line does not name it.
flags.say: Give an official body's advice as its own ('Australia's Alcohol and Drug Foundation says naltrexone does not work for everyone and advises talking to a doctor or drug counsellor').

flags.line: It can be found in blood and urine.
flags.why: Rests on one patient's blood and urine samples tested by the authors. It does not say how long 3-MeO-PCP stays or whether an ordinary drug test finds it, which is what was asked, nor that the sources are silent.
flags.say: Answer both halves plainly, how long 3-MeO-PCP can be found and whether a usual drug test finds it, and where the sources do not say, say so; one patient's tested samples are not a drug test.

flags.line: PCP can be seen in urine for up to 14 days.
flags.why: The 14 days is for PCP, a different drug, from the background of a report on false positives; placed after 'It', it reads as 3-MeO-PCP's time, and nothing says it is not.
flags.say: Answer about the drug asked about: a time given for PCP is not one for 3-MeO-PCP; if PCP is named, say plainly that it is a different drug and the figure is not for 3-MeO-PCP.

flags.line: A case report and review found 3-MeO-PCP in blood and urine, with a half-life of 10 to 11 hours.
flags.why: The half-life is what the paper cites from two other research groups, not what it found; and an unexplained half-life reads as how long the drug stays, which it is not.
flags.say: Give a figure a paper cites from others as cited ('two research groups estimated ...'), explain a half-life plainly (the time for half of it to leave the blood), and never give it as how long a drug stays.

flags.line: This rests on 1 review and 1 study in people.
flags.why: The second source is two case reports about false positives on a PCP urine test (how2 itself says 'Two case reports'), not a study in people; case reports do not carry an answer.
flags.say: Count case reports as case reports, and do not rest an answer on a report about a PCP test's errors: it is not a source on how long 3-MeO-PCP stays.

flags.line: Higher doses of D. stramonium can cause severe central nervous system damage, hallucinations, and death.
flags.why: 'D. stramonium' is the Latin name of jimsonweed, the plant asked about, and the line does not say so; 'central nervous system' has a plain word, the brain ('toxic syndromes' in how1 is poisoning).
flags.say: Write jimsonweed, not D. stramonium; the brain, not the central nervous system; and poisoning, not toxic syndromes.

flags.line: Yes, a 2022 review says datura is very addictive and leads to dependence.
flags.why: The quote does not name datura: 'They are very addictive' is plural, in the abstract of a review of several Nigerian plants. The answer's whole 'Yes' rests on that one sentence.
flags.say: Use a source's words only for the drug they name; where a review speaks of several plants together, do not give it as a finding about datura, and say plainly when no source speaks of datura alone.

flags.line: After smoking, the action starts fast and is intense. After taking it by mouth, it starts after a delay and lasts a long time.
flags.why: Compares ways of taking opium for speed and strength (smoked: fast and intense; by mouth: delayed and long), which the site never does; how1 and how2 repeat it.
flags.say: Never compare ways of taking a drug for how fast, how strongly or how long it acts; leave such lines out.

flags.line: After smoking, the action starts fast and is intense. After taking it by mouth, it starts after a delay and lasts a long time.
flags.why: The question asks first what opium feels like; the answer never says, nor that its one source (a review on blood sugar, fats and blood pressure) does not; 'a long time' gives no length.
flags.say: Answer what opium feels like, and where the sources do not say, say so plainly; 'a long time' is not an answer to how long.

flags.line: A 2024 review of fruit fly studies says functional tolerance comes from neurophysiological changes and can be acute, rapid, or chronic.
flags.why: 'Functional tolerance', 'neurophysiological changes' and 'acute, rapid, or chronic' are lab words a reader who left school early would not follow ('invertebrate models' in how2 means flies and worms).
flags.say: Say what functional tolerance is in plain words (getting used to alcohol through changes in the brain), and write flies and worms, not invertebrate models.

flags.line: Atomoxetine can be stopped abruptly without withdrawal effects.
flags.why: Reads as leave to stop a medicine suddenly, in the site's own voice, resting on one background line in the introduction of a review about combining ADHD medicines; and it is silent on the other non-stimulant medicines asked about.
flags.say: Do not tell readers a medicine can be stopped suddenly: give what a source says about stopping as that source's ('the introduction of a 2025 review says ...'), and say the sources speak only of atomoxetine.

flags.line: It depends. Regular use may lead to tolerance, but other sources say it does not appear to result in increased tolerance.
flags.why: 'It depends' names nothing it depends on: the sources disagree about regular use (Alcohol and Drug Foundation against NZ Drug Foundation), which the But says plainly ('mixed').
flags.say: Lead with what the sources show, that they disagree on whether regular DMT use builds tolerance, and keep tolerance within one lab session apart from tolerance over regular use.

flags.line: The NZ Drug Foundation says regular DMT use does not appear to result in increased tolerance, unlike LSD, and taking more results in stronger effects.
flags.why: 'Taking more results in stronger effects' tells a reader how to get a stronger effect; it is attributed, but given as a fact about strength, not as the foundation's warning.
flags.say: Leave out lines about getting a stronger effect from taking more; if an official body's warning is used, give it as a warning about the risk, in its own words.

flags.line: A 2025 study of 22 healthy participants found that people develop acute pharmacological tolerance to continuous DMT infusions.
flags.why: 'Acute pharmacological tolerance' and 'continuous DMT infusions' are lab words; they hide that this was tolerance within a single two-hour drip into a vein in a lab, not tolerance built up over regular use.
flags.say: Say plainly what was measured and where: in a lab, during a single two-hour drip into a vein, the body got used to DMT; that is not tolerance from regular use.

flags.line: It can.
flags.why: No quote says diphenhydramine gets anyone high: they speak of misuse, of children and teenagers overdosing to film their 'altered behavior', and of harm. 'It can.' answers yes for them.
flags.say: Say what the sources say: people misuse it in large amounts for its effects on the mind, and the US FDA has warned that more than the recommended amount can cause serious harm or death; never a plain 'It can.'

flags.line: Higher doses can lead to serious heart problems, seizures, coma, or death.
flags.why: Higher than what? The FDA's warning, given here without naming the FDA, says higher than the recommended amount; without that, it can read as meaning only very large amounts.
flags.say: Keep the comparison and the speaker: 'the US FDA has warned (a 2025 review reports) that more than the recommended amount can lead to serious heart problems, seizures, coma or death'.

flags.line: The NHS says taking more than the recommended dose is dangerous and can cause a fast heartbeat, seizures, or unconsciousness.
flags.why: The NHS says taking too much 'can be dangerous'; the line drops 'can be' and puts a stronger word in the NHS's mouth.
flags.say: Keep an official body's own strength: the NHS says taking too much 'can be dangerous', and lists a very fast heartbeat, a fit or passing out as reasons to call 999.

flags.line: A 2026 review found alcohol consumption and dependence were associated with neuropathy in people.
flags.why: 'Neuropathy' is a clinical word; the plain one is nerve damage. The line is also about a harm of drinking, not about whether alcohol is addictive.
flags.say: Write nerve damage, not neuropathy, and keep each line on the question asked.

flags.line: Fly agaric mushrooms look like red and white spotted toadstools. They contain chemicals that can cause severe or fatal poisoning.
flags.why: Asked what fly agaric is like, it says how it looks, not what it does; the review on people ('mild to moderate' effects, deaths rare) is left out, and the risk line rests on a report about poisoned ducks.
flags.say: Say first what fly agaric does to people, from the 2025 review on people (usually mild to moderate effects on the mind; deaths rare), not from a report on ducks.

flags.line: A 2022 narrative review of khat chewing says it increases blood pressure and heart rate. It also links chewing to dental caries and liver risks.
flags.why: 'Dental caries' is a clinical word; the plain one is tooth decay.
flags.say: Write tooth decay, not dental caries.

flags.line: FRANK says people can become dependent, especially with regular use. The NZ Drug Foundation says many find it hard to stop.
flags.why: FRANK says 'Research suggests' people can become dependent; the NZ Drug Foundation says many people who use them say stopping can be difficult. The short drops both hedges, which how1 and how3 keep.
flags.say: Keep each source's own strength: 'FRANK says research suggests ...', and people's reports as their reports ('many people who use them say it can be hard to stop').

flags.line: Cannabinoids work by interacting with CB1 and CB2 receptors, serotonin receptors, and TRPV receptors. THC binds to CB1 receptors in the central nervous system, which can affect perception, cognition, and motion.
flags.why: The whole short answer is in lab words (CB1, CB2 and TRPV receptors, central nervous system, cognition); a reader who left school early learns nothing from it.
flags.say: Say it plainly first: THC, a substance in cannabis, attaches to switches on brain cells called CB1 receptors, which changes how people sense, think and move; give other receptor names after that, explained.

flags.line: A 2023 review of literature on individual variations in response to cannabinoids found that CB1 receptors in the central nervous system are the main receptors responding to THC.
flags.why: This is the review's background section describing cannabis, not what a review about why people respond differently found.
flags.say: Say what a review's background describes as just that ('a 2023 review explains ...'), never as what it found.

flags.line: A 2025 review says in animals, opioid tolerance offers less protection against fentanyl's respiratory effects than for morphine or heroin.
flags.why: 'Respiratory effects' hides the safety fact in it: in animals, tolerance protected less against fentanyl slowing breathing than against morphine or heroin doing so. A plain word, breathing, exists.
flags.say: Write breathing, not respiratory: in animals, being used to opioids protected less against fentanyl slowing breathing than against morphine or heroin.

flags.line: 2C-B can be found in saliva for up to 24 hours.
flags.why: The study found 2C-B in saliva up to 24 hours 'in half of the volunteers' (16 people, measured in a study, not a drug test); the line drops that and reads as true for everyone.
flags.say: Keep the narrowing words ('in half of the 16 volunteers'), and say in the short answer that routine drug tests often do not look for 2C drugs (NZ Drug Foundation).

flags.line: It can stay 9 to 30 hours, and routine drug tests may not find it.
flags.why: 9 to 30 hours is loperamide's half-life, the time for half of it to leave, not how long it stays; the But ('prolong its stay') and how1 ('found a half-life') repeat the slip.
flags.say: A half-life is not how long a drug stays: say what it is in plain words, and give how long it can be found only where a source says so.
